target.title: Real-time decoding of question-and-answer speech dialogue using human cortical activity
target.version: Published Article; open access under CC BY 4.0

read.pdf: No PDF supplied; figures and tables were not visually read. The text extraction refers to figures and tables but does not preserve their contents.

entries.text: The study recorded three human epilepsy patients undergoing clinical treatment at UCSF.
entries.condition: Human patients undergoing epilepsy treatment at UCSF Medical Center; implanted ECoG arrays were already clinically indicated for seizure localization.

entries.text: Participants 1 and 2 each had two 128-channel arrays; participant 3 had one 256-channel array; participants 1 and 3 had left-hemisphere coverage and participant 2 right-hemisphere coverage.
entries.condition: Participant-specific clinical implants; participant 1: two PMT 128-channel arrays; participant 2: two PMT 128-channel arrays; participant 3: one Ad-Tech 256-channel array; participants 1 and 3 left hemisphere, participant 2 right hemisphere.

entries.text: The task used nine recorded questions and 24 possible spoken answers grouped into four question/answer sets.
entries.condition: Fixed, multiple-choice question-and-answer task; the four sets define which answers are valid for each question.

entries.text: Each testing block contained 26 question-and-answer trials.
entries.condition: Each trial consisted of a question followed by the participant's selected answer; the number of testing blocks per participant is not stated in the main text.

entries.text: During training, every question and every possible answer was repeated ten times in separate perception and production blocks.
entries.unit: repetitions per question or answer stimulus
entries.condition: Question training: participant listened to each question; answer training: participant read each answer aloud; speech detector used both block types.

entries.text: Question recordings lasted 1.38–2.42 seconds, with a 3-second onset-to-onset interval during question training.
entries.condition: Question-perception training blocks; the question stimuli were prerecorded by one female speaker.

entries.text: Answer prompts were shown for 0.5 seconds, cued green for 1.5 seconds, then removed for 0.5 seconds before the next prompt.
entries.condition: Answer-production training blocks; text and an image were displayed, and the green phase instructed the participant to read aloud.

entries.text: Testing trials were separated by 2–3 seconds of silence and a blank screen.
entries.condition: Testing blocks; trials were cued, with answers selected from displayed options.

entries.text: Fewer than 0.5% of trials were excluded for no response or an invalid answer.
entries.condition: Invalid choice or failure to respond during testing; excluded trials were omitted from further analysis.

entries.text: Arrays used disc electrodes with 1.17-mm exposure diameters and 4-mm center-to-center spacing.
entries.condition: Square-lattice ECoG arrays implanted on one cortical hemisphere per participant.

entries.text: Recorded neural data were sampled at 3051.76 Hz, then anti-aliased and streamed to the real-time computer at 381.47 Hz; audio was recorded at 24414.06 Hz.
entries.condition: DAQ recordings included time-aligned microphone and speaker audio; the streamed ECoG was the decoder input.

entries.text: The real-time filter bank used eight bands spanning 72.0–144.0 Hz, averaged into high-gamma activity, then z-scored over a 30-second sliding window and clipped to [−3.5, 3.5].
entries.unit: bands; Hz; Hz; seconds; z-score range
entries.condition: Per-channel ECoG feature extraction; high-gamma analytic amplitudes were averaged across bands and used in all analyses and real-time testing.

entries.text: Full-system utterance accuracy reached 61% for produced answers and 76% for perceived questions.
entries.condition: Best rates reported across three participants in offline simulations of the real-time system; accuracy is 1 minus utterance error rate for the concatenated test-block sequence and includes speech detection, utterance classification, and context integration. The participant attaining each maximum is not identified in the main text.
entries.quote: We decode produced and perceived utterances with accuracy rates as high as 61% and 76%, respectively (chance is 7% and 20%).
entries.loc: Abstract; Results—Question and answer decoding performance

entries.text: Reported chance accuracy was 7% for answer decoding and 20% for question decoding.
entries.condition: Chance was estimated from bootstrapped sequences of randomly sampled utterances, separately for the utterance-sequence accuracy metric; this is not the uniform 1/vocabulary-size baseline.
entries.loc: Abstract; Results—Question and answer decoding performance

entries.text: Question accuracy was 2.6, 3.1, and 2.1 times chance for participants 1, 2, and 3.
entries.condition: Question full-system decoding, each participant's concatenated held-out test-block sequence; chance from bootstrapped random utterance sequences.

entries.text: Answer accuracy with context was 7.2, 3.5, and 3.7 times chance for participants 1, 2, and 3.
entries.condition: Full-system answer decoding with question-derived context priors; each participant's concatenated held-out test-block sequence.
entries.quote: participant 1: 7.2, participant 2: 3.5, participant 3: 3.7 times the chance level

entries.text: All three participants exceeded chance for all three prediction types under one-tailed bootstrap tests with a four-way Holm–Bonferroni correction.
entries.condition: Questions, answers without context, and answers with context; participant-wise full-system accuracy; one-tailed bootstrap tests; four-way Holm–Bonferroni correction.

entries.text: Full-system answer accuracy improved with context for participants 1–3 (p = 1.9×10⁻³, 7.9×10⁻⁵, and 0.029).
entries.condition: Answer decoding with versus without context, full-system utterance accuracy; one-tailed permutation test with four-way Holm–Bonferroni correction.
entries.quote: participant 1: p  = 1.9 × 10 −3 , participant 2: p  = 7.9 × 10 −5 , participant 3: p  = 0.029

entries.text: Answer classification accuracy improved with context for all participants (p = 0.033, 1.9×10⁻⁶, and 9.2×10⁻⁴).
entries.condition: Classification used true event times from acoustic transcriptions rather than the speech detector; one-tailed exact McNemar tests with four-way Holm–Bonferroni correction.

entries.text: Answer cross-entropy improved with context for participants 1–3 (p = 7.6×10⁻⁶, 2.6×10⁻¹⁷, and 3.1×10⁻¹¹).
entries.condition: Classification and context-integration likelihoods over test-block trials; one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with four-way Holm–Bonferroni correction; lower cross-entropy is better.

entries.text: Question and answer speech-detection scores were above 85% for all participants, but imperfect.
entries.condition: Speech-event detector; score combines frame-by-frame accuracy and event-count accuracy, averaged across test blocks for each participant and utterance type.

entries.text: Production-phone classification accuracy was 25.12% over 10,585 speech time points; the evaluated phone set contained 37 phones.
entries.condition: Answer phone-likelihood models pooled over all participants and test blocks, at time points during speech production; chance was calculated separately.
entries.quote: there were 10585 time points that occurred during speech production, and the overall phone classification accuracy across these blocks was 25.12%

entries.text: The production-phone chance level was 2.70% when choosing among the 37 phones.
entries.condition: Random single-phone choice for the answer phone-classification analysis; silence excluded from the stated 37-phone test set.
entries.quote: the chance level was 2.70% if choosing randomly from the 37 different phones

entries.text: Including silence yielded 50.97% phone classification accuracy across 165,804 time points.
entries.condition: Pooled answer phone-classification analysis across participants and test blocks, with silence time points included.

entries.text: Phone-confusion mutual information across nine place-of-articulation categories exceeded randomized categorizations (p = 0.0012).
entries.condition: Production phone labels were collapsed into nine disjoint place-of-articulation groups; silence token /sp/ excluded; one-tailed bootstrap test.

entries.text: For 94 correctly classified answer trials pooled across participants and test blocks, neural-based decisions typically finalized before speech offset (p = 2.1×10⁻¹⁵).
entries.condition: Answer classification trials correctly predicted by the answer classifiers; one-tailed single-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test of decision finalization time.
entries.quote: these decision finalization times for each trial in which the answer classification models correctly predicted the produced answer (94 trials total across all participants and test blocks)

entries.text: Transcription-based finalization was before speech offset (p = 1.6×10⁻¹⁶), and neural-based finalization was later than transcription-based finalization (p = 1.2×10⁻¹⁰).
entries.condition: The same correct-answer trials; one-tailed single-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test for the transcription lower bound and one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank comparison of neural versus transcription estimates.

entries.text: Classification improved over approximately 10–15 randomly drawn training samples per utterance, corresponding to about five minutes of speech data; saturation was not established.
entries.unit: training samples per utterance; minutes of speech data
entries.condition: Participant-specific utterance classifiers were evaluated on all test-block trials; samples were randomly drawn from training perception or production trials.
entries.loc: Results—Effects of data limitations and hyperparameter selection

entries.text: Speech-detection performance plateaued with about 25% of available training data, as little as four minutes including silence.
entries.unit: % of training data; minutes including silence
entries.condition: Speech event detector, each participant; comparison used increasing amounts of available training data.
entries.loc: Results—Effects of data limitations and hyperparameter selection

entries.text: Hyperparameter optimization evaluated 250 epochs for each participant, model type, and held-out test block using leave-one-block-out cross-validation.
entries.condition: For each test block, the associated validation set comprised the participant's other available test blocks; best validation performance selected that block's hyperparameters.

entries.text: Question classifiers trained on repeated listening data, answer classifiers on repeated spoken answers, and event detectors on both types of training blocks.
entries.condition: Participant-specific models trained offline on time-aligned high-gamma z-scores and phonetic transcriptions, then saved to the real-time computer.
entries.loc: Results—Overview of the real-time decoding approach; Methods—Modeling

entries.text: Audio was phonemically transcribed with p2fa, then phone boundaries were manually fine-tuned in Praat; question and answer sets each contained 38 unique phones, though the sets differed.
entries.condition: Phone-level supervision from time-aligned audio; includes a silence token /sp/; transcriptions were created after data collection.

entries.text: Event detection used selected electrodes, spatiotemporal high-gamma features, PCA, and shrinkage LDA; speech-event labels were perception, production, or silence.
entries.condition: Training event labels came from phone-level acoustic transcriptions; hyperparameters controlled electrode inclusion, feature windows, PCA variance fraction, smoothing, and onset/offset thresholds.
entries.quote: the speech event at time t and is one of the values in the set {perception,production,silence}

entries.text: Each candidate utterance was represented by a phone-state HMM; PCA-LDA estimated phone emission likelihoods and Viterbi decoding produced utterance likelihoods.
entries.condition: Separate question and answer classifiers per participant; detected neural segments included silence states at utterance boundaries, with self-transition and next-phone transition probabilities.
entries.quote: During testing, we used Viterbi decoding on each HMM to determine the likelihood of each utterance given a detected time segment of high gamma z-scores

entries.text: At use time, decoded question likelihoods updated fixed context priors: valid answers within that question set were equally likely and answers outside it had zero probability; answer likelihoods were combined with these priors.
entries.condition: Context prior encodes the predefined relationship between the nine questions and 24 answers; prior influence is scaled by an optimized parameter; no external language model is described.
entries.loc: Results—Overview of the real-time decoding approach; Methods—Modeling—Context integration

entries.text: The system outputs one identity from the fixed question or answer vocabulary, selecting the highest-likelihood question and highest-posterior answer.
entries.condition: Closed-set decoder; answer options were displayed to participants. The system did not generate unrestricted speech or text.
entries.quote: the answer with the highest posterior probability was output as the decoded answer (Fig. ).
entries.loc: Results—Overview of the real-time decoding approach; Methods—Experimental task design

entries.text: The authors report that answer classifiers could finalize correct predictions before the end of the produced utterance using neural phone likelihoods.
entries.condition: Correctly predicted answer-classification trials; classification analysis used true speech-event times, separate from full-system detection.
entries.quote: the answer classifiers were able to finalize classification decisions before the offset of speech using estimated phone likelihoods

entries.text: The authors claim a novel real-time paradigm decoding both perceived questions and produced answers in a task designed to resemble natural dialogue.
entries.condition: Three human participants; externally cued question-and-answer task; not spontaneous free conversation.
entries.quote: there have not been attempts to decode both perceived and produced speech from human participants in a real-time setting that resembles natural communication

entries.text: The authors claim that integrating the decoded question as context significantly improves subsequent answer decoding.
entries.condition: Question likelihoods constrain the answers for the associated QA set; improvement was tested against answer decoding without context and observed in all three participants.
entries.loc: Abstract; Results—Question and answer decoding performance

entries.text: The authors describe their paradigm as an advance over prior isolated listening or speaking tasks and as a major step toward more naturalistic decoding.
entries.condition: The authors' novelty comparison is qualitative; no head-to-head performance comparison against prior systems is reported.

entries.text: The authors argue that HMM/Viterbi decoding is robust to variability in phone duration, pronunciation, and small onset/offset errors.
entries.condition: Methodological rationale rather than a quantitative comparison against an alternative decoder.

entries.text: The authors present the results as a step toward a speech neuroprosthesis for people unable to communicate, not as a demonstrated clinical prosthesis.
entries.condition: Study participants were epilepsy patients with temporary clinical ECoG implants, and the tested task was closed-set cued dialogue.

entries.text: The authors concede that participants received external cues and timing, so the task remains less natural than free dialogue.
entries.condition: Testing included an auditory question, visual answer choices, and a green response cue; answers were selected from displayed options.

entries.text: With only three participants, the authors say they could not make quantitative, definitive claims relating decoder performance to functional-anatomical coverage.
entries.condition: Between-participant electrode coverage and decoder performance; authors identify this relationship as potentially important for electrode placement.

entries.text: Because of clinical time constraints, optimized hyperparameters were not used during bedside testing; reported performance comes from offline simulations, while online performance was not quantified.
entries.condition: Online bedside decoding used trial-and-error hyperparameters; the paper reports no online accuracy values, only no systematic/runtime errors and negligible latency.

entries.text: The authors acknowledge that visible answer options could have influenced visual or language processing, although they had no evidence of such an effect in this study.
entries.condition: Answer choices were visually presented; participants chose among those options during testing.

entries.text: The authors note that transfer to imagined or covert speech is uncertain and may require different phone models and training procedures.
entries.condition: The tested system decoded audible perception and overt spoken production; imagined speech and fully paralyzed participants were not tested.

entries.text: The authors concede that current data volumes limit effective use of more powerful neural-network decoders, while phone labels only approximate the underlying articulatory representations.
entries.condition: Clinical data collection was limited; richer training data or articulatory descriptions may improve decoding.

entries.text: Speech-event detection was high-scoring but not perfect, and the gap between full-system decoding and event-time classification indicates that better detection could improve overall performance.
entries.condition: The full-system accuracy includes event detection; classification-only analyses used true event times from acoustic transcriptions.

entries.text: The authors state that hyperparameter choice substantially affected classification performance and that clinical time constraints prevented optimizing models before online testing.
entries.condition: Offline primary results selected parameters using held-out test blocks in leave-one-block-out optimization; online bedside parameters were selected by trial and error.
entries.loc: Results—Effects of data limitations and hyperparameter selection; Methods—Real-time decoding

entries.text: Using hard predicted-question context did not improve answer predictions; true-question context improved classification for only one participant, not significantly for the other two.
entries.unit: participants with classification improvement under true-question context
entries.condition: Auxiliary answer-classification analysis using hard priors or the true presented question instead of soft decoded-question likelihoods.
entries.loc: Discussion; Methods—Evaluation methods and statistical analyses—Auxiliary decoding analyses

entries.text: The authors caution that the training-sample analysis does not establish how much data would be needed before performance stops improving.
entries.condition: Classification improved through approximately 10–15 training samples; performance did not fully plateau except for participant 2's answer classifier at 30 samples.
entries.loc: Results—Effects of data limitations and hyperparameter selection; Discussion

entries.text: The authors identify participant-specific electrode coverage, alertness, and task engagement as possible sources of performance variability.
entries.condition: Only three participants with different cortical coverage; no quantitative attribution of performance differences to these factors.

entries.text: The authors report an online bedside demonstration with no systematic/runtime errors and negligible latency, but provide no quantitative online accuracy result.
entries.condition: Bedside online testing used trial-and-error hyperparameters; all reported accuracy results derive from offline simulations.

entries.text: The main text does not report the number of testing blocks or sessions per participant, although it points to a supplementary table for training and testing data amounts.
entries.condition: Testing blocks have 26 QA trials each; counts per participant and session organization are absent from the supplied article text.
entries.quote: Information about the amount of data collected for training and testing with each participant is provided in Supplementary Table .
entries.loc: Results—Overview of the real-time decoding approach

entries.text: No random seeds are reported for bootstrap resampling, random training-sample draws, random block order, or the Tree-structured Parzen hyperparameter optimizer.
entries.condition: Applies to stochastic training-sample selection, task randomization, bootstrap tests/resamples, and optimization reproducibility.
entries.loc: Methods—Experimental task design; Methods—Hyperparameter optimization; Methods—Evaluation methods and statistical analyses

entries.text: No held-out participant or cross-speaker evaluation is reported; classifiers were fit and assessed separately for each participant using that participant's training and testing data.
entries.condition: The same participant identity occurs in training and test data; question stimuli were recorded by a single female speaker and reused, so neither participant-independent nor question-speaker-independent generalization was tested.
entries.loc: Results—Effects of data limitations and hyperparameter selection; Methods—Modeling

entries.text: Although leave-one-block-out validation is described, the main text does not identify the individual block assignments, the number of blocks available per participant, or the resulting training/validation/test counts.
entries.value: block counts and assignments not reported in main text
entries.condition: For a test block, all other available test blocks formed its validation set; model fitting used separate training blocks.

entries.text: The 30-second sliding-window z-score normalization is specified, but the initialization, data used to initialize/update its statistics, and reset behavior between blocks are not stated.
entries.value: initialization / reset / statistic scope not reported
entries.condition: High-gamma analytic amplitudes were normalized with Welford's method over a 30-second sliding window and clipped to [−3.5, 3.5].

entries.text: The authors define chance estimation by bootstrapping random utterance sequences but do not state the number of chance-sequence draws or a random seed for this estimate.
entries.value: draw count and seed not reported
entries.condition: Chance accuracy for full-system utterance-sequence decoding; the separate one-million resamples reported for classification accuracy and cross-entropy means/variances do not specify chance-estimate draws.
entries.loc: Results—Question and answer decoding performance; Methods—Evaluation methods and statistical analyses

entries.text: The main text does not identify which participant attained the headline maximum answer and question accuracy rates of 61% and 76%.
entries.value: participant mapping not reported in main text
entries.condition: Abstract reports best observed full-system accuracy; participant-specific ratios to chance are given, but not the absolute per-participant rates in the extracted article text.
entries.quote: We decode produced and perceived utterances with accuracy rates as high as 61% and 76%, respectively
entries.loc: Abstract; Results—Question and answer decoding performance

entries.text: The paper reports comparisons to chance and to answer decoding without context but no quantitative head-to-head comparison against an external ASR or neural speech-decoding system.
entries.condition: The qualitative novelty discussion cites prior approaches but the paper's primary evaluation uses within-study chance and context/no-context comparisons.

entries.text: No user confirmation step for the decoded question or answer is described.
entries.condition: The decoder outputs the most likely question and answer directly; no user-facing accept/reject interaction is specified.
entries.loc: Results—Overview of the real-time decoding approach

entries.text: No user correction mechanism or online adaptation from corrected outputs is described.
entries.condition: The system selects closed-set utterance labels; the paper describes no correction interface, user feedback, or correction-dependent retraining.
entries.loc: Results—Overview of the real-time decoding approach

entries.text: Classification accuracy was above chance for every prediction type in all participants (p < 0.05, one-tailed bootstrap tests with four-way Holm–Bonferroni correction).
entries.condition: Question, answer without context, and answer with context; classification used true event times; one-tailed bootstrap tests and four-way Holm–Bonferroni correction.

entries.text: Means and variances for classification accuracy and cross-entropy were estimated from one million bootstrapped trial resamples.
entries.condition: Resamples of trials for each participant; this count is reported for accuracy and cross-entropy estimates, not for the separate chance-sequence bootstrap or its seed.
entries.loc: Methods—Evaluation methods and statistical analyses—Primary evaluation metrics

entries.text: The nine questions were prerecorded by one female speaker at 44.1 kHz; the participants produced answer utterances themselves.
entries.condition: The same prerecorded question stimuli were used in training and testing; no question-speaker holdout was evaluated.

entries.text: Question selection during each block was weighted by the number of valid answers in each QA set.
entries.value: questions with more valid answers had greater selection probability
entries.condition: Testing blocks; exact selection probabilities and per-set test counts are not stated.

entries.text: Classification-only accuracy used transcription-defined true speech-event times and padded each classified utterance with 300 ms of silence before and after it.
entries.condition: Question and answer classifier evaluation on test blocks; this bypassed the speech-event detector and was separate from full-system decoding accuracy.
entries.loc: Methods—Evaluation methods and statistical analyses—Primary evaluation metrics

entries.text: The event detector's frame-accuracy score weighted positive frames at 0.75; its overall score weighted frame accuracy and event-count accuracy equally at 0.5 each.
entries.unit: positive-frame weight fraction; frame-score weight fraction
entries.condition: Speech-event model optimization and detection-score evaluation; positive labels were expanded by 300 ms around transcribed speech events.
entries.loc: Methods—Evaluation methods and statistical analyses—Primary evaluation metrics

entries.text: Classification accuracy and cross-entropy were above chance for all participants and prediction types under one-tailed bootstrap tests with four-way Holm–Bonferroni correction.
entries.condition: Classification used true test event times; cross-entropy used predicted likelihoods; questions, answers without context, and answers with context.

entries.text: Real-time classification of heard sentences from ECoG with direct sentence-level and HMM phoneme-level schemes; listening only.
entries.condition: Two epilepsy patients listening to repeated sentences; closed set of ten sentences.
entries.quote: Subjects listened to multiple repetitions of ten sentences, and rtNSR classified what was heard in real-time from neural activity patterns using direct sentence-level and HMM-based phoneme-level classification schemes.

entries.text: Two epilepsy patients took part.
entries.condition: UCSF epilepsy patients.
entries.quote: The two subjects (A and B) who participated in this study were human epilepsy patients undergoing treatment at the UCSF Medical Center.

entries.text: Single-trial real-time sentence classification accuracy of 90% or higher for each subject with under 7 minutes of training data.
entries.condition: Ten-sentence closed set, perception, each of two subjects, real-time classification.
entries.quote: We observed single-trial sentence classification accuracies of 90% or higher for each subject with less than 7 minutes of training data, demonstrating the ability of rtNSR to use cortical recordings to perform accurate real-time speech decoding in a limited vocabulary setting.

entries.text: Stimulus onset came from an audio onset detector that injected a start token, not from neural speech detection.
entries.condition: Perception task; timing from the played audio.
entries.quote: This sound triggers an audio onset detector in the preprocessor to inject a start token into an arbitrarily chosen recording channel.

entries.text: No language model at use time; language modelling is named as future work.
entries.condition: Closed set of ten sentences.
entries.quote: In future work, we plan to expand the HMM-based classification scheme into a real-time continuous speech decoder that uses language modeling and Viterbi decoding (similar to a real-time version of the system described in [ 10 ]).

entries.text: Seven epilepsy patients with ECoG grids.
entries.condition: Albany Medical Center; produced speech.

entries.text: Participants read text aloud (overt production).
entries.condition: Production task.

entries.text: Gaussian ECoG phone models combined with a pronunciation dictionary and an n-gram language model in a Viterbi decoder.
entries.condition: Offline phrase decoding from produced speech.
entries.quote: Combining these Gaussian ECoG phone models with language information in the form of a dictionary and an n-gram language model , the Viterbi algorithm calculates the most likely word sequence and corresponding phone sequence .

entries.text: Word error rates as low as 25% and phone error rates below 50%.
entries.condition: Offline, best case across seven participants; produced phrases.

entries.text: Evaluation was offline.
entries.condition: All evaluations.

entries.text: Viterbi decoder over LDA phoneme likelihoods with an n-gram phonemic language model, for perceived speech.
entries.condition: Listening task, offline phoneme decoding.
entries.quote: The system implements a Viterbi decoder that incorporates phoneme likelihood estimates from a linear discriminant analysis model and transition probabilities from an n -gram phonemic language model.

entries.text: Speech-detection and word-classification models from cortical activity in attempted speech.
entries.condition: One participant with anarthria; ECoG; 50-word vocabulary.
entries.quote: Specifically, we created speech-detection and word-classification models that used deep-learning techniques to make predictions from the neural activity.

entries.text: Real-time sentence decoding with a natural-language model and a Viterbi decoder.
entries.condition: Sentence task, 50-word vocabulary.

entries.text: Median online word error rate 25.6% at 15.2 words per minute.
entries.condition: Real-time sentence task, 50-word vocabulary, with language model.
entries.quote: at a median rate of 15.2 words per minute, with a median word error rate of 25.6%

entries.text: Conversational demonstration: prompted with a statement or question, the participant responds with words from the 50-word set.
entries.condition: Conversational variant of the sentence task.

entries.text: Offline isolated-word classification accuracy 47.1% with detector and classifier, no language model.
entries.condition: 9000 isolated-word attempts, offline, 50 words.

entries.text: Day-1 accuracy 99.6% on a 50-word vocabulary after 30 minutes of attempted-speech training data.
entries.condition: Intracortical, 256 electrodes, one man with ALS, attempted speech, 50-word vocabulary, first day.
entries.quote: On the first day of system use, following 30 minutes of attempted speech training data, the neuroprosthesis achieved 99.6% accuracy with a 50-word vocabulary.

entries.text: Day-2 accuracy 90.2% with a 125,000-word vocabulary after 1.4 more hours of training data.
entries.condition: 125,000-word vocabulary, second day.
entries.quote: On the second day, the size of the possible output vocabulary increased to 125,000 words, and, after 1.4 additional hours of training data, the neuroprosthesis achieved 90.2% accuracy.

entries.text: 97.5% accuracy sustained beyond eight months.
entries.condition: Large-vocabulary use beyond eight months after implantation.

entries.text: The conversation partner question is transcribed from audio and supplied as context; answers are selected via EEG code-VEP.
entries.condition: Non-invasive EEG; question from automatic transcription, not from brain signals.
entries.quote: The conversation partner asks a question, which is automatically transcribed and supplied

entries.text: Authors state that all reported results are offline simulations with the rtNSR system.
Bedside online decoding ran without systematic/runtime errors and with negligible latency, using trial-and-error hyperparameters.
Authors argue offline results would equal online ones because only hyperparameter values differed.
Authors have no evidence that visual presentation or reading influenced results and propose testing without these aspects.
Restricting answer predictions by the predicted question (hard prior) gave no performance improvement.
Real-time computer: Linux machine (Ubuntu 14.04, Intel Core i7-4790K, 32 GB RAM) running rtNSR.
In BCI spellers, language models give a prior over target characters from the user's previous selections.
entries.quote: These models can provide a probability distribution for target characters based on previous selections, which can be used as a prior probability for future selections.
entries.loc: Sec. 2 (review of Speier et al. and others)

questions.q: Free-model reader runs on the four priors (Moses 2018, Herff 2015, Moses 2016, Moses 2021) timed out without answer.json; specific passages were taken by targeted grep of each source text instead.
questions.answer: Entries p1-p5, h1-h5, n1, l1-l5 hold the passages.

questions.q: Triage: authors' offline disclosure, hard-prior wording, visual-cue caveat, M13 system description, and Speier-style speller priors (pmc-5495144-lmbci) — taken by targeted search of the source texts.
